One reason is:tbat unlaaptised children are thought to be at the mercy of fairies, and sub- ject to the influence of the evil eye. Another fancy is that, should a drill die unchristened, it is destined either, to flit restlessly around its parents' abode, or to wander in wood+ and lonely places, daily lamenting its bawl fate. In Scotland it is said to le unlucky to give the child any name until after bap. lieu; and even now-a-days in many country places a, child is invariably called by the name of the saint on whose fes- tival it IDAT happen to have been born ; any orniwion of this practice being supposed to bring ill consequences. Hence not unfrequently children are found with very strange names. It is a very COIOIIIIO2I notion that a child does not thrive until baptised, and in cases of illness the clergyman I. perhapv more frequently sent for by the poor from a belief in the physical virtue of the rite itaelf rather than from any actual conviction of its religions importance. It is considered a good omen for a child to cry at its baptism, as otherwise it shows that the baby id too good to live. Martin, in his " History of St. Kilda," tells we that it was customary for the inhabitants always to baptise their chi'. demon a Saturday, from a superstitious notion that if this ceremony were observed on another day they would die. , An odd idea prevails in Norfolk, that when there are girls I and boys to be legaised, the boy moat come tirst, or else the girl will hare a beard. In Scotland, when a booby was car- ried to church to be baptised, it sea', considered important that the nurse appointed for this purpono shoold he known lobe lucky. She generally took with her a piece of bread. and-chee., which she prwented to the tirst person she met '—this representing a gilt from the baby. If the party readily accepted and ate the proffered present, it was a goal omen ; but if refused, it woe considered tantamount to with- 'mg evil to the child ; and in after life, if any rnidortune betel the child, it was invariably associated with this cir. cumstance.—Leince A Bengali writer, Jo ;endaranath Bidvahhushan, hos re- cently published in the vernacular a Lite of Maasini, to- gether with a abort account of Itali. history, hie object being, as he mys, to excite patriotic feelings among the ilindoos, and to teach them to prefer the good of their country to their self-interest.

It 6 stated, however, by Professor Verrill, in the 41. i-wan Journal of Sdence, that the Peabaly ?duscom at Yale College has Ltely received some fragments of white Italian marble from a cargo wrecked off Long Island in 1871, not taken up in 1878, in which the exposed nor- Cons of the dale are thoroughly penetrated to the depth of one or two inches by the crooked and irregular borings or galleries of the sponge Mena sulphurea, and reduced to a ceinplete honeycomb, readily crumbling in the fingers" Be- yond the borings the marble WAS eaid to be perfectly sound and uceltered. Chemically viewed, theee are confounds of silica, magnesia, lime, and oxide of iron. They differ from other varieties of hornblende chiefly in containing little or no alumina, and are remarkable for assuming a fibrous charac- ter, the fibres being sometimes very long, line, and flexible, and having much the appearance of flat. They form corn- pact masses, but can often be easily separated by the fingers 'They vary in colour from white to green and light brtwn. One yuiety of utlestos is known ss "mountain cork," or rook cork," being soft like cork, and no light unto tent on water. Another, called mountain letther," or " rock leather," is found in thin flexible sheets, with interlaced fibres, and is also lighter than water. " lgounmin wool" is more compact, and brown in colour, remembling dried wood There are some filgous varietiee of serpentine which are often confounded with asbestna Thin is not to be wondered at, as asbentos it not unfrequently found in serpentine for. mai an..f., Work. . .

The tar in not generally worked up in the gas works, but is aold to the tar diatillers, who separate it by distillations and rectifications into several products the benzines or benaele, naptholene and anthracine, being the products utilised in the production of dym. These producte generally leave the tar distiller, and then benzines are either ! sold to ihe colour work. or to the manufacturer ra aniline, I who, after coeverting them ieto nitrahersols, oLtain the aniline by treating the latter with reducing agente, using iron filings and acetic or moriatic acid so that the products which am really the raw materials for the manufacture of colours are the benzole, naptholene, and anthracine, the two latter being generally aold to the dye manufacturer to be purified and afterwards converted into colours. An EVENT TO Currros.—The Chief Entomological Com- mieeimier to the United Staten has, according too Southern dmpatch, lost addressed the Cotton Exchange at Mobile on the subjmt of the cotton worm, now threatening much dam- age to the growing crop. The worm, the caterpillar of an owlet moth, is of triangular dupe, about an inch long, the upper wings of a reddish grey, and the under wince darker. It hss sixteen legs ; but the feremoet are so ehort that in creeping it arches the back like a epan-worm. The colour is green, with light yellow stripee and ..look dots alon' e the back. It grows often to the length of an inch and a half. Its eggs ere Len to fifteen, deposited on the under surface of the tender leave, which thee rmenib:e in colour, aed to which they are firmly attached. Incubation lasts from six to fifteen days, depending probably on the degree of heat ; thr young grows rapidly, and begins very early to not. The skin is changed several time. before the insect hoe attained full growth, 15 to 20 days, after which it ...es to feed, forming an imperfect cocoon of a leaf and silk. In this the ehryealis state is past—from 10 te 12 days—after which the moth lays he egg., and dies in about a week, though it h. been held that it survives mild wintere. The worm is ex- ceedingly destructive in some yearn, having occasionally Cot off the entire cotton crop in certain districte. Its ap- pmr.ce in often no midden and u.coouritable that it is thought it must migrate from the South. Its harmfulnees wee first noticed about 80 a-ears ago, since when ito ravages have been almost every year more or Is serious. Some persons believe that the worm appears in the rme districts at intervals of three years, and that its greatest miachief or done every 21 years. At lend, 1004, 1825, and 1546 were memorable in this regard. It may appear any time between June and October. Moderate cold will kill it, though moim torn and high winds ...m no have no perceptible effect. While it devout, with entire impartiality the long and short staple, it aeldom touches any other plant When it in found early in the se.on it is apt to hare three brood,. It prob- ably originates in South America, and when the last brood has expired, either from cold or hunger, it is supposed that it leaves no progeny behineL

Walter was-;-u-n-g and etrong /le had among omen- tains inn beautiful land. One day he set forth, staff in hand, to climb the Mountains. It wee a lovely summer day; The trees .st their shadows on the rade of the mountains . birds sing in their branches. Little ills of water trickled over, rocky hale on their way to the alley ; dower, grew tracery bank ; and the bean of the voting man glowed within iihn as he stepped front one be.tutiful object to an- other.

Often had he heart of this dower, which blooms bat once in seven years, and then .mly for a mingle day. He gathered It and set it on his breast, and then renewed his walk with steps more active than ever. He had climbed a long way from where he began ; but to the top the way was longer still. Iligh above him wand the peak of the mountain. Rougher and steeper grew the path. At last it ended al • tamer breast of rock. Walter sighed. Was le to fail an n•ir the top? He maw a strong tuft rooted in a cleft of the rock. He seized it ; he sprang tip the steep. As his body !swung to and fro, the Lock-donor on his breast touched the rock, and no moment there was a hollow moan, a splitting open of the stone wall, and the entrance tot mighty cave. Hat still more wonderful, when he looked into the cavern he found it full of all precious tbings—gold and precious stonee, moors red nt..l green and yellow and purple. And there ' were diamous spukling clear as water from the spring. Never before had such rlchee been seen by himn.ncner had he even dreamed of such. And it was no dream, but reality. A step farther, a step into the cavern, and he could touch the gems. Ah, if now, at that moment, he had lifted up his heart to God and said, Lead me not into temptation, bet deliver me from evil," how different this adventure would have beer' Hut Walter in a moment forgot God, forgot the beautiful mountain he was climbing, forgot the Luck- flower which had so filled him with joy, forgot trees and flowers and songs of birds, and all the happy, innocent, joyous life that God had given him, fastened his eyes greedily on the riches at hi. feet and on every side. tan moment he might be rich. And in a moment he stepped down into the wondrous cavern and began to fill his puckets, his breast, and at Lud his cap, with the rubies and diasoonda and gold. If you had seen him now ! He was not the same bright and happy youth as when he set out in the morning. The face of youth was gone. The face of care was In its Mao, He had become in one hour a miser, a boarder, with DO thought, among all 114 thoughts, but thin—. It Is the one good for nie to gather these richea."

If this greed for gold and precious stones had only left him room to think, he would have known that it was the voice of the Luck-flower which had dropped out of his breast. It was the Luck-Bower which had opened the mountain for him, and by which he had leen admitted to all thin wealth. Beat it was nothing to him no.; he had forgotten it. He despised everything no. cept the gold and the pr!eiti.us stones:

Another step, and he would he out- side. But that other step was never to be taken. He had left his guardian angel behind him, on the tloo,f the cavern. It had m ened the door for him ; it could have kept it open till he was oat. But it no locgcr on his bresst—oot even kept in mind. W.dter came up to the entrance. FRANCE. . . .

In a letter to the Archbishop of Parts, the Pope protests against the expulsion by the French Government of the non- ' authorised religions communities from their domiciles. The Pontiff regrets that the French Ministry did not accept the , declaration of these confraternities, especially as the declare- Goo, he says, was originally suggested IT the Government itself. The French Ministers, at A Cabinet Council on Tues.- I day, resolved to resume the ent,cement of the decreee against the on-authorised congregations in the province.. It appears that up to the present time 110 of the estah- lishmente belonging to the religioue orders in France have ' been closed under the authority of the March decrees. A singular incident is reported in connection with the enforce-1 ment of the decrees at Rennes, where the military were mm- mooed to the aid of the civil power. One of the infantry officers, it seems, refused to obey the order, and sent in his resignation, which war, however, refused by the War Minis- ter, to whom the case had been reported by the General in command, and the officer is to L. brought lAfore a court I martial. . . .

Pants,Thursday.—Tbe enforcement of the March decrees Win continued to-day in all parts of the country. At Angers the fathers of the Holy Sacrament and the Capuchins were ejected from their establishments, Mgr. Treppel, the Bishop leaving with the Capuchins. At St. Etienne, ale, the Capuchins were expelled from their monastery at Havre, the Dominicans at Valence, the Redemptorists at Anton, the Oblates at Cabers. the Capuchins at Orleans, the Manias at Meyers, the Oblates at St. Annielain, Premontre, and Penner, the Dominicans at Bourges, the Franciscans at Besancon, and the Capuchins. At each of these places the police had to force the doors of the religious houses, and in every ease a formal protest was made against the action of She authorities. In sorest towns the police hail to climb through the windows in order to gain an entrance into the monasteries. At Dijon the First President went to the Com- missary of Ponce, 1010 WO superintending the expulsion of the Dominican, and asked by whose orders he was acting. The Commissary showed his order from the Prefect, and de- clined to stain the names of the locksmiths and masons whom he was employing to force the doors of the Domini- cans' house.

(Animals) Act, liArii; suggesting that farmers cud graziers should be reminded of their duty,l under the act of Parliament, to give immediate notice to the police of any outbreak of the disease, and isolate any sus- I pected animals ; an I pointing out the importance of exer- cising strict supervision over markets and fairs, and other places where animals are exhibited, with the clew to animals being subjected to careful inspection by qualithd officers.

The CLEM( submitted the following propoul to the Board have to submit for the consideration of the Guardiaoe the desirability of their praviding a horee and cart for the removal of the poor patients from the several districtsof the Union to the Workhouee, and also of lunaties to and from Rainhill Asylum. The relieving officers' books show that during the vear ending September, MO, the sum of .03 7e. was wended inob hire. and a further suns of 120 is spent annually in hor. hire Many of the persons removed are suffering from a loathsome and Infectious discs., and I am not aware that any crepe are afterwards taken to disinfect the carriage, and I am afraid that the cab- man would not care to inform his return tare of thecondition of the former occupant of his conveyance. A second-hand brougham might be purchased for about £3O, and the horse need not coat more. There is ample stable accommodation at the Workhouse, and several of the inmates are capable of acting as coachmen It would, non matter of public-health, be a preventative of the epread of infectious die.se as well as a saving to the Union. ERFIELD. The monthly meeting of tide members of the Board was held on Wednesday. Mr. A. B. Mouhert presided, and there were also present the Rev. 11. 5i.1.1.111, Messrs. 3. Gaskell, Lowe Latham, Richardson, Burchall,Boardman,and Rigby, J. F.:Fairless (clerk). W. tioldsworth (surveyor), 3. Hill (collector), and T. Chambers (sanitary inspector). The Chairman introduent the question of the mode adopted by. the Assessment Committee of the Beard of (dirndlsn, of essessing colliery property in the township of Ashton. Ile pointed out that through adopting the system of areraaes .•' ' "

instead of fixing the assessment on the rental the rate- payers had lost no less than .£7,441 Ile 3d. in the last been years, or an average of £2,480 IN. a year. In addition to that sum they had lost on the trespass rent, which was separate from the rent on coal and not introduced in the assessment at all, in the same peridd, £.921 11.44. If a similar state of things was in existence in the other town- ships in the union the lose to the ratepayers in a series of ' Yeats would be immense. Several members concurred in the remarks of the chairman, and the matter was Adjourned to the next meeting.

FATII/511.—At the Manchester Amiss,. on Tuesday, before Sir John Mellor, Samuel Oldham, 34, was sentenced to twenty-five years' penal /servitude for at- tempting to murder his eon, William Thomas Oldham, aged ten years. at Rochdale, on Sunday. the 19th September. About ten o'clock at night the prisoner took the boy ton secluded spot on the bank of the river Roche, and, while the little fellow was picking up by his father's orders a match which he had let fall, the prisoner pushed him into the water And runaway. The boy sank, but on coming to the !surface he succeeded in scrambling to the opposite bank, where he pulled himself out. Wet and dirty with the mud of the Goer, the boy roamnl about the fields all night, and at ten o'clock next morning he wee takes in and kindly treated by • Mrs. Clough. On Sunday afternoon, 'several hours before the event happened, and while the boy seas etanding at his side, the prisoner wrote to the mother of his wife, from whom he was separated, telling that "Willie" bad been missing sometime, and on the same night he went to Rochdale Police Station and told a similar story. The Judge said there were circumstances in the case Which re- minded them of the old records of the criminal courts. If the prosecution was rights more deliberate, wicked, and artful cam Bever came before a court of justice.

The fight for mceicipal hceoure at Warrington on Monday was conducted on purely polities! grounds . We have previously explained why politic. were per- mitted to exercise so great an influence in the muni- cipal contest this year. The Liberal., feeling that they had a majority among the elector., art demon• ✓ated by the great victory they achieved in April lad on the mention of the election of a member Si represent the town in Parliament, and being in the minority in the Town Council, made • requer to the Coneervative that the latter should concede to them an allernanship md oouncillorehip (both of which were about to become vacant because of the voluntary retirement of en alderman and a statutory cation of a councillor) in order to prevent the town being put to the expense and turmoil of • contest. it was confidently hoped in the early ragee of the nego- tiations which took place that the request, which, if °model, would still have kept the Laved. in the mino- rity in the Council Chamber, would meet with the ap- proval of the rank and file, as it did with the venally rearogniced leaders, of the Conservative party. Thir confidence, however, was misplaced, and, the nage- rations being broken off, both sides prepared for • great struggle for the mastery. The prism to hi fright for were nine councillorships, with • pro.pect of having the Choice, on the 9th met., of • gentleman to fill the office of Meyer, and of foar others to di.. oh srge the duties of aHernren, that number of rats becoming vacent on the 9th. Lush being promoted to the Court of Appeal, and in Mr. Welkin Witilseso, Q.C., tho present member for Carnarvonshire, being raised to the dignity of a puisne judge in the Queen's Bench Dirioion. Sir Watkin Williams, as he will now be called, fought in April hut a memornble political battle in the Welsh coanty, and beat by more than a thousand votes the son of Lord Penrhyn, who wait supponed to be all- ntrerful in the county. Sir Welkin Williams, who ia a son-in-law of Lord Chief Justioe Lush, recently refused the office of Judge Advocate General, and his elevation to the Queen's Bench Division is one that will give matiefaction to the whole legal profession, as ho is accounted not merely a good speaker but an ex- salient lawyer. Dreaustannis are, by virtue of the Tolerstion Act, still " tolerated; " and it is not to be wondered at that occasionally there should be an out buret of dis- content that, in the eye of the law, they are held to exist only on eufferance. The present ecclesieetical lawe stamp one met of religionists, and that not the most numerous in the land, with a supetiority over all others, and these statue., stand on the legisletive roll as a perpetual insult to a vast body of well- ordered and male. Chrietions. In the dark ages, when religious bigotry was made a stepping-stone and • cloak for greed and gain, atatutee were enacted against battier., marriagee, and hernia being mlo- heated or performed in pima, other than the religious edifices protected and favoured by the State. The burial laws have reeently had a serious breach made in their exclusiveness, and before full equality end fuetice can be eetablished they will have to be stripped of provisioee which give to the clergy of the Estab- listiment • kind of overseership over the interment of Dissenters in Nationsl churchyards. Prior to 1836 no reaming. in England were legal which had not taken place in n Church of the Establishment, and when the Regiatration and Marriage Bills were introduced into Perliament, the Fetablishel clergy, who feared a! nductioa of amplice fees, predicted no exten- sion of Atheism and constant religion. the. • content in the land. Though by the Marriage Act of 10116 the celebration of weddings in Dissenting plame of worship, if licensed for the purple., was Showed, it net only in that spirit of "toleration" • which gave birth to the Toleration Ant in the days of William 114. It was decreed that a marriage in a • Dieeenting &ape' should only have the sanction of the law if it was performed in the presence of a regie- trar of marriages, but that functionaryle presence was not deemed necessary in a State Church to legalise a marriage taking place therein. An instance of till. insulting "teleran." and religious inequality haM joet occureed at Blackpool. In a Dissenting chapel a few days ago mrangemente had been made to celebrate • marriage, and t half •past ten in the forenoon the miniater, the Rev. S. Pilling, the bride, bridegreem, andtheirfriende, werepresent. Thechapelwascrowded with spectators, but the wedding could not be pro- ceeded with bemuse of the absence of the registrar. The Rev. 8. Pilling considerately explained the canoe of the delay, but that made matters worse. Sem }Wed the situation of the couple anxious to be made "happy." Others more windy tried to make out why on earth a Dissenting minister might not be toasted to register the limninge he was deemed fit enough to eelebrate. Meesengers were sent in all directiens to eeek the miming registrar, but, as his maidens, was four or fives miler away, there was not tame to seek been before the clook strimk the hour of men. At slew mined., to twelve o'clock, the Rev. Mn. Pilling tried to appeue the wrath of the assembly by sugge.ting that there must have been some mis- tuadorstanding. They were realising that morning, he said, one of the penalties of being Dissenter.. Thu emotion forood itmlf home to them, se, perhaps, it had rimer done leforim—'. Why should • mrvice like that be dependent upon the attend.on of a regis- trar?. Re wee ready to proceed with the teenier, suds thousand people were ready to witue.n to its validity, and yet, beenuie a registrar was not present, after all ritir preporationit the matiriage most be delayed to mother day. A etron ger exemplification of the inequalities ender which Dissenters suffer could hardly be couseived tlian this marriage incident, nor a stronger reason supplied for putting persons of all religions opinions upon an equal footing in the eyo of the law.

ISome time ago, I believe, a reference was made, in one of the reports of a meeting of the Runcorn Imigovement Conn. missioners, to a suggested purchase of the gasworks at tame future time. It may interest those whoare in favour of such A scheme to be told that a few days ago, on the opening of a beautiful fountain at Birmingham, to cornmetnorete the noble work which Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., had done for the municipality, it was stated in the address presented to that gentleman that during the five years which had Fused since the Corporation acquired the property of the Birmingham Gar Company no less than £134).000 had hero emtributed in a direct form to the rates from the gas department. Of course, every year that the Rundorn works remain in the powtession of the present company, their ehare capital increases in value ; and it hardly needful to say the they know this quite all well AA the ColllllllSaiollera, Wiuterly weather le now upon or in right good earnest, , and, hmtead of getting to work and completing the proposed improvement at Waterloo Bridge, the Cominissionere com- mittee are apparently busy trying how not to do it." It It pretty well known that, owing to the subscription to the Runcorn Young Men's ehrietitu Association being placed , ' at such a low figure, the place has to he conducted at a low Indeed, so indifferent are many of the rich men of Runcorn , to whether the rooms prosper or not, that if the committee relied upon their yearly subscriptions, they might shut up to-morrow. Scarcely a large religious public meeting is held but one may hear aome doleful Matements made as to how the churches are losing the young men, who are going back into the world "; and yet the wmlthy religious people of the town continue to hold on with the firmest possible clutch to "the sitter." Talk is cheap, and there is far too much of it. There would not be so many yousg men found in the billiard rooms of our large hotels, which are too expensive places for them to frequent, or in very , questionable places of amueetnent where gambling ie openly ! carried on, if the religious professors were a little more liberal and not eo eectarian in their way of looking at things. , Those who wieh to see what eta be done to attract young men around a religious institution should visit the magniti- clone rooms of the Young Menk Chrietien Asexiation, in Peter-street, Manchester, and they would come away with the idea that if all other towns, according to their power, were to act in the eame manner, many young men who gat into had way. would be retained as useful members of society. It,. only • few weeks ago that Mr Robert Shaw had to hand the committee of the Runcorn Association • chequo for abaut4o/ to pay off their liabilities. All honour to Mr. Shaw for his noble and well placed generosity; hut what many of the young men of the town are asking iv how is it that members of other Large firms are so in- different to tho finsuciel position of a nociety which isdoing so pod a work. On looking at the annual reports it will be eeen that the subscriptions given by gentlemen of influence in the Runcorn religious world are miserably email.

The idem which some workmen have as to the property of their employers are ttuiymn.tentraordinory. Men whose notions as to honesty are all right on other matters, will frequently take possession of small amount, of material for which their masters has paid in good coin of the realm and coolly appropriate tbem to their own use. This sort oi thing no doubt arises, in some cams, front the pomession of • peculiar sort of conscience. I have met with men, and many of them possessed of no special clevernese in their particular calling, who appeared to believe that the laws of political economy as to wages were most unjust towards them, and that it was not atoll unfair for them to do thmng. with an employer's goods or materials which they would have been the first to strongly resent if they bad been in the position of master. These hleas.pa,eed tlitottglt toy mind on hearing of noose tried at the Widnes Sessions this week, in which a workman employed by one of the largest firms in the place had 20s. and costs to pay for taking sin staves f wood, value 2d., from the premises of las masters for the purpose of making a bird cage. CHAPEL. anniveroary sermons were preached in the above chapel oe Sundt), sot to good congregations. The sermon 11Ithe afternoon was preached by the Rev. Breckenbury, In the absence (through indismaition) of the Rev. F. S. Hagen, hut in the evening tho latter gentleman had so far recovered aa to be able to .leliver • powerful sermon from Luke 10e 42,. The collection on behalf of the trust fund mallow' • Ellie over £6. A pshlic mooring was held on Monday coming when a largo somber of person. eat down to • capital tea. After- wards the Res. E. O. Coleman preeided, and there vrerd alm prentrat Meows. W. Y. Lawton, E. Ford, W. Gleam, S. MAN, E. J. finest, 8.A., W. Collier, It. Garnett, IL Garnett, Wurnmersgill, Weaver, dm. The Cnotanur, after • few remarks, called upon Mr J. Srmirenenird., who gave a very intermitting accongt of the history of Methodiem at Sankey Bridge.. He Mid lltilodopsndent ethodlete, of Warrington, were the irst to no into their midst • little more than 40 years ago, and they preached ins small cottage. They afterwanl. hired • hens. which obtained the name of the Old Meeting Hoene, and here they conducted service, beside. holding • school for tie instruction of the young. The mum, however, failed, and fffattkey Bridges was left to its fate. The Primitive Methodist, next turned their attention to the plan, and for twelve months preached on Sundaye, hut they Mao, for want of eaccess, retired. Then the Wesley. Methaliste lifted vp theo standard. About twenty years ago the the. dame. Laycock, the then superintendent of the Warrington Crrmait, came down to reconnoitre and he gained the sym- pathy mid help of their old friond Captain Eskdale. They found favour with the late Mr. Joeeph Reed, whew housn. wee opened for preaching, and Mr. Joseph Howard, of Sankey Hall, preached the dew sermon. The efforts put forth were very succeasful and about four years ago it was. thooght desirable to provide increased accommodation to inset the requirements of the increasing population, by eventing the preernt chapel and schwd. The result of the labours that had stare been bestowed upon the place had v ery encouraging, Ind he trusted that In the future they would meet with still greater success. (Applame.) M., W. Y Layrron then delivered an address upon "the )440 and iM influences." Mr. E. Form in speaking of "The local preacher: hi. work," referred to the labours of the remarkable early Methmliet preachers, whose eanctided )nernories he said wonld never perish while Methodiem existed. What would the mnnexiom have been to-day if it had not been forth. help and for the assietance of local pre.hers? Local preachers had kept Methodiem alive in villages—(hear, hear),—to-day they spoke the Word of Life in thousanda of pulpits, and they furnished the ranks of the regular minis- try with recruits. (Hear, hear.) lie was glad to under- stood that Methodism since its commencement hod not been without witnessee, but that there had always been a number of gad, righteous, and talented men to step into Oho minis- try to preach the Word of Life unto the people, and taking them altogether, both the local and travelling preachere, there was not a grander set that day under heaven. Laaghter, and appistme.) In 1740 Nonconformity existed in the proportion of four toevery hundred pereons, to-day Non- cantor. ity stood nearly forty to every hundred,—(hear, hear)—and he thought they would come to the cenclmion that men like those on that platform had been the mean. of doing • great work in the land. (Applause.) Mr. W. Oceans lelivered a capital address on "What are the best means to protrude a revival of religion in our cirenit," and urged upon the audience the necessity of being of one seeded. . .

Mr. S. Moss spoke of the " Methodist outlook," and said wino they looked at their put history and present position ha believed they had every reesou to take courage. (Ap- plause.) It sus not long since John Wesley began his choreh, and now his followers formed the largeat church in the world. What were the aspects of Methodism now? They bad uhibited a noble spirit of liberality, and they hail greatly improved their church architecture, and given inanseeed chapel eccommodation. The anixct in that cieenit we.,. changed that they would hardly know it from what it on ten years ago. Another upect wee the increased it/elation giver to the young people. (Hear, bear.) They would all admit the importance of that, because that church which eared most for the young, would unquestionably be the cherch of the future. (Hear, hear.) 'Their only hope lay in the young people, and he rejoiced to no. that they were waking up to that great fact. They were alai making .n 3 attempt to provide their young people with good, cheep, healthy literaturs--(hear, bear); giving more attention to , the Sabbath echool, and increased attention to the Band of Hope. (Hear, hear.) This he took to be one of the healthy signs of the age. They were giving their attention to home. tressioas—(hear, hear,)—end he hoped they woulrl ever , maintain their aggressive work. There wee not adequste, provision now for public worship for the population of the, country, and he was thankful they were going to them. They were going to the masses with the schoolmaster, and they ought to go to them with the Gospel. That would require • special effort, end until they recognised individual reeponsibility they would fail in their miesion. lie was' glad they were waking up to the necessity of keeping alive Methodiern in villages, and in conclusion asked them to try to keep themselvw alive in the work. (Applause.) Mr. E. J. Gran, 8.A., spoke of "The valee of the Oater ineetlng and the importance at efficiently maintaining it." Alter referring to the social sympathetic feeling in man, he said that Church was lacking which did not provide come means for the extension of the feeling. John Wesley was one of the wiseat men that ever lived, and he gave to them the claw meeting. (Hear, bear.) He now that the Chmch must be consolidated and strengthened, and there was better way of consolidating and strengthening than by the clus muting. (Hear, hear.) There were live reasou why he thought the clans meeting a valuable inetitntion. It pro- moted freemasonry amonget the members, and there wee • freemasonry amongst them that they could find in no other church. The class meeting was well adapted for teaching the truths of God's holy word, and was an inetitution which developed Christian character. The class meeting was well adapted for the discernment of Christian gifts end graces ; and they owed it to the class meeting that they had such a pore, such • practical. nen an experimental and powerful ministry, both local and itinerant. (Hear, hear.) Again, the claw erecting had been well adapted for cultivating a spirit of generosity amongst the people, and if the class meeting did those thing, it watt worth maintaining. There were clergymen of the Church of England, there were men like the tt,, R. W. Pale, of Birmingham, the foremost amongst the Congregationalists, who would gladly attach the inatitntion to their church if they could, and should they let it go? Gal forbid. In order to maintain it let them speak respectfully of it. (Hear, heir.) The class meeting ehould he maintained as a test of membership, and if it meet be maintained efficiently it must he maintained by making it natural and profitable. (Hear. hear.) The great desMn was that they might become easy and natural in their convereation abeut the deepest things which pertained to their peace. If it wee to he profitable they must prepare for it, and if they did this they 'meld maintain the class meet- ing and maintain it efficiently. (Applause.) Mr. Comvan gave en addrees on the" Circle of Mello, , diem." The Methodist circle which be spoke of IVA, the world, and they were represented in eve-y prelim, of the world. Methodism we. ersentially missionary enterprise,' and when it ceased to become a missionary organisation, ' whether in home or foreign missions, then its 'access would droop and it would die. (Hear, hear.) The circle was still widening, and John Wesley's motto het,! good, "The friends of all ; the enemies of none." 1

111,11 Usarerrr Mill he had always thought a great deal of the local prmcherw ant he thought more of them now than hefure,—(hooo, hearl—and he proposed that the best thanke of the meeting he given to them for their excellent addreesee. (Applause.) Mr 0•01101? &mum seconded the metion, which waa heartily carried. A vote of thanks to the chairman for presi ling brought the meeting ton close.

STRANGE SUICIDE OF A WARRINGTON YOUNG MAN. THE INQUEST. it the White Hart Inn, Sankey-Street, on WedneednY afternoon lest, Mr.C. E. Driffiald,the county coroner, opened an inquest OW the body of George Jobe Dean, 21 years of age, who died at the Warrington Infirmary, on the let of November, from inguriee inflicted with a revolver. Mr. U. Elinston acted as foreman of Ole jury. The first witnesa called was: Edmund Hughes, 41, Winwick-street, foreman porter at the Central Station, said be was on the platform when the 6-60 train, on the 26tb ult., arrived from Manchester. Ile ear, the deceaaed turning the handle of a third-elass com- partment, previoue to getting out of the train. He wart smoking at the time and got out himself, when witness saw a wound on the right aide of the temple, from which Mood wait dropping. Wilmette thought be saw hint place a revolver in his side pocket as he was coming out, and said to him.. What have you been doing S Have you alma yourself 1" and he replied, 'Ye,.' It. was then handed over to Inspector Thompson. There watt blood on the tloor of the , vgriage. Inspector Thompson, of 30, Hopwood-etreet, Warrington, said hewas an inspector at theWarringtou Cemral Station. On Tuesday evening, the 26th ult., he received the 6-50p.m. express from Manchester, when his attention wee called by the last whores to the deceased. He was walking along the: platform, bleeding from a wound in the right temple. Witness heard Hughes ask the deceased if he had shot him- self, and he replica yes. Witness saw decesteed'e hand in his pocket, and pulling it oat found that he was clutching a : revelver,•everal of the chambers of which were loaded. Its also took out from him pocket a box containing slumber of pistol cartridges. Witness then rent for a polieernan, and took the deceased in his office when he was asked what he had done it for. Deceased maid he had been on the race- course, adding that he shot deliberately to kill himself. Alfred Cokely, a constable, said he was on duty at Bewsey road end, when • porter from the station said that hie services were wanted at the Central Station. Wilneas pro- ceeded there and found the deceased In the office of Mr. Thompson bleeding freely from a wound in the right temple.. To hie questions the deceased replied that be shot at himself with a revolver as he was coming from Manchester to War-1 rington. Witness searched him and found two small ; memorandum books in his pocket containing a number of I entries of bete apparently of horse races. H,. asked him if be had been betting heavily on tile" Cambridge," and he raid, "I have a little." Witnees aleo saked him if he Was led to attempt to commit suiaide by anything relating to hie duties, and he said, No, its something worse than In one of his coat pockets he had a nnmber of cartridges. He woe then taken to the infirmary, the deceased walking all the way. Charles E. Richmond, house surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, said that a little after seven o'clock on the 26th ult. the ;leceased was brought to the infirmary. He hull thorn a bullet wound ia his right temple. In reply to quee- lions, he said he was • telegraph clerk and lived in Cairo-st. He mid he had shot at himself with intent to kill, and the first ,hot had gone onto! the window. The brain was ex- tensively injured, and on there mortre examination being made witness found a bullet lodging in the left half of the brain, front which death had resulted. It was marvellous how he had lived as long as he did. Witness questioned him on several occasions as to the reason why he shot himself, hut could gain no satisfactory reply. E. B. Bowser, the master of the Warrington Post Office, and the deceased had been employed for the last five years in the telegraphic department. Ile was always steady and well-conducted, and his attempting to commit suicide was not on account of anything connected with the office, as he had no connection with mosey matters. The Coroner said he had no hesitation in cooing that tbe deceased died from wounds inflicted by himself. Yet they had no evidence of sanity or insanity, and lathe absence of such he ehould direct the jury to bring in an open verdict. lb. boo. for MONTROSE, in an able speech, com- pared the class of education given on the Continent, notably in Prussia, with that given in England, and, referring to its optional character, said that boys there were forced to pass a certaM examination before being permitted to wrk. He should like to see such a tation M the English system. The him member for Nmecasme-ox-Tven, in a humorous epeech, criticised the remark of the hon. member for Truro that the Church catechistn was unsectarian. As a child he had learnt, good deal front that particular catechism, and he thought he was entitled to say a few words about it. Ile found that the teaching of the catechism worked : improperly as it inculcabd wrong ideas into the children's minds. Ile once got Mtn trouble for saying. in answer to a minister, that his father and mother gave him his name. He was answering according to the mtechism, and was corrected by the minister, who told him that he was named by his godfather and godmother. As a matter of fact he had no godmother or godfather until he INAS ten years of age. (Laughter.) It had the effect in that COO of making him give an answer at variance with truth, for the rake of adhering to the cate- chism. Ile considered the catechism of the Church of Eng- land to be purely sectarian, and he could not support the motion, because he did not agree with the propoeition that school attendanee committees should he invested with the full powers of a School Board. The hon. member for Wesx CHESHIRE gave his sepport to the measure. . . . . .

—.Boman Exmostow ETA PARIS BATH Two LADIES Dungan no lisarn.—A terrible accident occurred on Wed- neolav night, at the great bathing establishment in the neighbourhood of the Ternes. The boiler burst, destroying the gas pipe around, and the gas igniting set fire to the establiehment, which. abounding in wooden partitions, burned with great rapidity. On the first door were two men in baths, .41 on the second door two ladies. The attendant, who had, as motel, I..cked the bathers up in their chambers, in the panic forgot to open the doors. Mr. T. COOK eupposed that as he happened to be one of the circuit stewards in the St. Helens and Breseol circuit it fell to his lot to give a very brief account of the objects of the tutelar and the circumstances which 'orought it about. They sought to raise a fund for the purpose of paying off certain disabilities incurred in refurnishing three of their ministers' houses. It might be aTo utter of surprise to many friends who were not intimately connected with Methodism that they should have to furnish their ministers' houses, while almost ail other ministers provided their two furni- ture thennselves. But it happened to be one of the distinc- tive features of Methodism that no emitter could remain in the same circuit for more than three years, except under very special circumstances; and it would be obvious to all that it would be most inconvenient, if not absolutely imprac- ticable, for ministers to provide their own furniture, as they had I. go through all meta of the kingdom. It was, them. fore, in the economy of Methodisin to provide them with all the necessary appliancea for housekeeping. It would be no matter of surprise Brat goods in a minister's house sore out, equally with the goods at their own houses—l hear, hear)— and for some considerably tine they had felt that the furni- ture and the household goods of their ministers required complete renovation. About twelve months ego the stewarde felt they ought to face that subject, and they did no with considerable trepidation, owing to the depression in trade and bad fimos. but such was the feeling in the matter that they expressed theasselvea to the effect that nos only was the comfort and convenience of their minietem at stake but also the credit at their stewards, and they were determined to face it. It was brought officially before a properly conetituted meeting twelve months ago, sad that meeting endorsed the views of the stewards. That bazaar woe, there- fore, the rtsult. They .nade an appeal throughout the circuit, end he might just state for the information of those who did not know, that the St. Helens and Breacot circuit ranged from Preecot and Itainhill on that side of St. Helens, to Haylock. Golhorne. Earlestown, and Burtonwood on the other aide of St. Helens. They made an appeal to these places, the response had been given by the grantl and tag. nificent display of goods before them, and a tight hearty response it was. (Cheers.) It might bee matter of enquiry as to how much they wanted to raise, but instead of going into figures he might say that they wanted to sell all the good. at a reasonable price, and as far as they could they had done what they could in the way of hop:easing upon the ladies the necessity of reasonable prices. ((thee found it otherwise, he, for one, would be disappointed. He, like Mr. Harry, presumed that they had got a good deal of money in their pockets. If they had a congestion in the pocket or in the purx, they would find a reedy meane of relierin, themeelves by patronising the various stalls. If they could not obtain reheat the first stall they could go to the next, and by the time they had got round the room, the, would find that the congestion had gone, end that they had got value for their money. If the complaint should return upon them they could come again on Wednesday, and If they then found thee were not cured. they could try again on Thureday. (Cheers 1 The ladies would be able to cure them and mod them away satisfied. (Cheers.)

He was afraid the fault in a great memure lay with those who ought to be their guides, and it was • verf serious question to consider. He felt connstrained to say—and he was sorry to have to my it—that the present state of accommodation in the churches and chapc s in St. Helens was really a most rnoinu,ri &ellen upon them. One heard in these days a great deal about Christian unity, a very nice thing if it was only brought about, but to talk about one form of worsbin, and to an. one form of Church government should be the universalfy recognised one was very peutile. "Many men, many mind,' was an old proverb. Their idiosynerasim varied; some liked one form of service, and some another. :Esthetic, reqnited a service which some would consider as fastidionn, whilst °there of • demonstrative and sympathetic man., like their Primitive brethren, would prefer a service accordingly. If they went I into Scotland they would find there many people who sat down to sing, and stood up to pray. He believed the same thing prevailed to a large extent amongst the Prmbyteriane of Germany. He could remember, and no doubt some of those present, two of their St. Helens worthies now at rut— end there meet perhaps few more worthier now alien —who always stood up at prayer in the Independent Chapel. He stated that they expected shortly to have an interview with Major Baring., the new Finance Minister for India, when they would bring under his mtice the confiscation of goods and the excessive penalties levied at India. ports on traders because in bales of cloth pieces were found containing yarn of finer counts than j those allowed by the Act, and also thesubject of the remain. , Ina italic. on cotton imports. Some discuseion took ;dace . on the Indian salt tax and ita effect on the purchasing power I of the people and the postdating of inrices. • -'

THE IRON AND COAL TRADES IN AMERICA.—A ECIISME which will have a moet important bearing on the coal and iron markets of the United States for the miming year, bas just been developed. Some enterprising RUNRAES have concluded to work the enormous coal fields of their country, and have associated themselves with a eyntlicate of American capitalists for this purpotc. It is said that the construction of a large number of miles of railroad has been found necessary in the developing process, and that over 500,990 tons of steel rails will be needed. American manu- facture, are of opinion the bulk of this iron will be Liken from the English market, and that inasmuch as the entire domestic production of the States will not exceed 900,000 tons, and that the importa in 1881 must be very small, owing to the scarcity of English rails, there will be an enor- mous appreciation in the price of steel rails. The present price is abaut $69, and enure heavy sales were concluded at that price during the early part of fast week. Taw LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—There it more activity in the iron market here, but any having is almost entirely confined to forward delivery, °enamors thisdistrict being mostly fully covered for their present requiremente, and where ironic pressed for immediate delivery very low prices are taken. There are inquiries for deliveries over the whole of next year, but where business is done makera as a rule are not disposed to go beyond the first three, or at the most the first six months, of next year. Some fair sales of local foundry iron have been made up to the end of March next , at prices ranging from 413 e. Bd. to 475. ed. per ton, less 2i , delivered equal to Manchester, and if Lancashire makers were prepared to book up to the end of dune a considerable quantity of iron could be placed. With regard to outside brands coming into this dietrict, there is still a good deal of pressure to sell Lincolnshire and Derbyshire irons at ex- tretnely low figures, which art considerably under those quoted for local irons, and this is keeping Middlesborough iron almost entirely out el this market, north country brands being only inquired for where specially required. Amongst finished iron makers rather more ordere are in some cases reported lobe coming in, hot generally there in no very material change, and prices continue low, the average quota- tions for local lure deliverAl into the Manchester district being about £5 17t. &I. to Ea per ton. Amongst pipe foun- ders and rockers at heavy castings in East Lancashire there appears lobe rather more doing. TIER LANCASHIRE Com- TIEADE.—For all classes of round coal suitable for house-lire purposes a good demand is, re- ported throughout the district, and in most cases the pits are now working full time. With Inc commencement of November there bat been a pretty general ups ard movement in prices. lathe Manchester district this has been chiefly confined to the delivery rates for house coal, which in some oases have been advanced 10d. per ton upon last month's quotations, and tote advance of sd. in some of the wharf price,; hut in nearly all the other Lancashire colliery dis- tricts] the pit prices have been put up. circulars having been sent out from a number of the collieries announcng ad- vances ranging from &I. to Is. per ton upon screened coal. Although it can scsrcely be said that there it a Inn advance all through to this extent, generally colliery proprietors are getting CM. per ton more for their house-fire coals than they were in September and October, and best coal at the pit ' month is now quoted from As. &I. to Os. per ton, with seconds ranging from Bs. &I. tale. &I. per ton according to quality. Common screened coal for steam and forge purposes, how- ever, .Icee not yet command any much txtter price, and there are ,till plenty of sellers in the market at from ss. 3d. Iv Sc. &I. per ton at the pit. Engine classes of feel are without material change, but the tendency, as pointed ont previously, is towards lesa firmness iu slack, which is now becoming plentiful in the market. For good burgy about Is. to 4e. BA. per ton at the pit is quoted, and for good slack 3s. to 3s. &I per ton. The shipping trade has been dull, owing to some extent to the scarcity of vessels; but apart frotn this there is no large demand, and no very material ad- vance upon late rate. is being obtained.

THE STATE OF IRELAND.

GOVMII.IT Puovr.ccrtows.—lt isolated that the indictmeeta against the land leaders were lodged on Tun- day. The indictments, each of which has • dozen COMM, contain extracts from speech. made at land meetings eines January last. Notice will be served to-day on all the defendant., and within four Jays they will have to enter an appearance in court. The following I. given a.. complete list of the defendants, but the almost eecrecy is maintained by the officials .—Mr. Parnell, M.P., president of the Land League; Mr. Biggar. MP.; Mr. Dillon, M.P.; Mr T. D. Sullivan, hi'.; Mr. Sexton, M.P.•, Mr. A. P. Kettle, Mr. J. Brennen, secretary to the Land League; Mr. I'. Egan, honorary secretor,; Mr. Sullivan, assistant secretary; Mr. Horton, Mr. Healy, Mr. Walsh, and Mr. Mathew Harris. The chief charge is that of conspiracy. Evidence will be given that the defendants acted in concert, and ordered placards to be printed for the league meeting., epeeehee at which ale included in the indictment.

iViit-1&;ci-;;;;;;.2fh.e"r;i-die;Vnts egsinst the land , Leaguers in Ireland are published. The informetions are exceedingly voluminous, and corer over one hundred closely Printed pages. The venu is laid in the county of the city at Dublin. There are 10 countein the indictrnents, and the charges are generally of conspiracy to defeat payment of rents, to prevent letting of forme from which tenants have been evicted, and to excite ill.will amongst Her Majesty's subjects in Ireland. The aubmenas were iesued on Weds.- day, and four days, in accordance with the ordinary rule, will be allowed for the traversers to plead. SERVING OF TIID lerinc-narmvs.—ln Dublin, on Wednes. day, the detective. were engaged in serving copies of the In- dictments upon the Land Leaguers. Mr. Parnell wasserved at the Imperial Hotel, Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., at the NationoMce, Mr. Brennan at the League Office, Mr. Sexton, M.P., and Mr. Egan at the Land League Offices. VIOLDNI ADDlass DT A Pnarnsvegr CLENOTMAN.—On Wednesday night the Rev. W. Stewart Roe, incumbent of Christ Church, Belfast, delivered the second of a coarse of lectures, entitled "Foe God, Queen, and Country. Proles. tants, awake!" In the course of his lecture the reverend gentleman said the Boman Catholic religion wean lie that the Irish national system of education was a seed of error when established, and that it had now grown to • great tree, which was striking its room into the Britielt Constitution and making a great rent. The Intermediste Edacation Act Waco sop to Cerberus, but it did not satisfy him, and the hellhound still hungered. The rev. gentleman arraigned Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Bright as land agitators in the Cabinet. In proof of this he quoted Mr. Gladstone's Mid- lothian speeches and Mn. Bright's recently publiehtd letter. He demribed Mr. Gladstone ass traitor to God and his country. GREAT LAND Marrlno.—Tl,. meeting at Tipperary, on Sunday, was attended by 10,000 or 12,000 people. The Very 1t,.. Dean Quirk°, P.P., Cashel, presided. Rettolu- tie. were adopted demanding the abolition of the present land laws, expressing gratitude to Mr. Parnell, and unalter- able adherence to the undying principle of Irish indepen- dence, the improvement of the condition of the agricul- tural classes, expressing abhorrence at the deeds of violence prove lent M England, and calling on the Government to use its utmoet power for the suppression of those abominable criines.—The Chairman said that there mass necessity for grmt caution. They were not afraid, but they would be cautious. The Government might threaten, and might arrest their leaders, hut others would stand up in their places.—Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Shaughnesey were present, and spoke.—Mr. .1. Costello°, an agricultural labourer, in moving & resolution, said that there were clergymen on that platform who would contradict what Dr. Moran had maid when be declared that the spirit of the gospel was not opposed to landlordism. WALSH AND 118 ALT en I'llisOn.—Mes.rs. Wale!, and Healy appeared at the Bantry eessions on Monday, to aaswer the charge of intimidating Cornell. Manning, and by threats end menaces endeavouring to make him leave his form. The magistrates, after hearing the case, committed the defendants for trial, but intimated their willingness to liberate them on bail. They declined the offer, preferring to be taken into custody, with the object, it isstated, of sub- eminently bringing an action for false iinprimminenf. INTIMIDATING Senn/rm.—Several servants end workmen In the employ of Mr. Barber, Doolnugh, have received anonymous letters, directing them to quit their employ- ment. because some herdsmen were recently discharged by It,. Barber.

LONDON RADICALS AND MN O'Conwou, MT.—A deputa- tion from the I. ndou &wheal clubs assembled at Easton Station, on Monday evening to present an addresa to Mr. T. P. O'Connor. MT., who was leaving for Dublin, with the avowed intention of there awaiting MB B.otlClP3ted arrest. The address, expressed the warmest thanks for the courage displayed by the honourable gutter., and asked him to convey to Mr. Parnell their aense of his ability as leader of the Irish Mono Rule party. Mr. O'Connor said he was going to attend the trial of Mr. Parnell, to whom was due the solution of 100,000 of his country men from famine. He would telegraph to Ireland he woe urrying the good wishes of London Railkals.

I'ItarBSTANT MURDER CLrBS.—Mr. A. M. Sullivan, M.P., hae written letter to the Chief Secretary for Ireland, in which he contends that if the Government are about to in- stitute prosecutioue for inflammatory language, tiCr um of tha Rev. Mr. Rune, who is said to have advised the forma. lion of murder clubs by Protestants by way of reprisal, ehould be dealt with, before any other prosecutions can be approached. Tun Corr or Moviro POLICF IN lustarn.—A parlia- mentary return shows that the toed cost to Ireland for the movement of military and police, rendered necessary by party processions in that country, sin. 1872, has been 1.58,253. Nearly the whole of the amount expen led retain Ulster. In Belfast the cost WAS £17,815 ; in Armagh, £12,143 ; in Ldndonderry, £IOAN3 ; in Down, £8,453 ; in Tyrone, 24,332; and smaller 11.13 were wended in ether , towns. The return gives the details of the expenses, many of them king in connection with C martyr" funerals, but by far the larger number were in connection with Nationalist and Orange processions. Til• "Ilevln's Barman," arr.. Cnrwcw Oral/Pro MIT Poucgwer.—The baliff in charge of a farm near Craughwen, from which the tenant was evicted, attends mass guarded by armed police. On Monday a placard was posted outside the chapel, calling on people to protest against this insult, and to keep that Devil'. emissary " out of the,cburch till he had withdrawn from the farm.

On Sunday two armed men entered the house of Edward Turrell, Edenderry,and threatened his life if he executed an ejectment against his eon. The son has been arrested. IN.: TY TO Tun QUEEN MY Mn. Mooned —At a meet- ing of the Land League, in Dublin, on Tuesday, Mr. Red- path said he was at Clonbur when Lord Mountmorres was killed, and knew everything about the transactions, as far as a journal* could learn, without taking an active part in it. The Queen, for whom he had very little respect, bad given a suite of apartments in the fashionable poorhouse, called Hampton-court Palace, to Lady Mountmorres; but the friends of the Irish peasantry had been far too gentle in their talk about this infamous rascal. He was a small edition of Lord Leitrim, one of the most corrupt magistrates that ever cureed a country. He bragged that he react Go- vernment spy, and made very disrespectful remarke about the Fenians. Another account says that Mr. Reepath made statements in reference to the murder of Lord Mount- morres,oome of which are unfit fer transmission. He Coen- located upon statements made on the subject at the Belfast meeting, and, alluding to Mr. Gibson, M.P., late attorney- general, as "this man laibeon," remarked that he had stated in Belfast that a number of young men who were peasants waded through the blood left on the road by Lard Mountmorres. That was 'len utter infamous, aleolate, damned lie." Lord Mountmorres was a stnall edition of Lord Leitrim, and the statement that a band of men had gone to where they sump.* the body of Lord Mountmorres lay, and played a funeral dirge. woe an abeolute, brutal lie. Lord Mountmorres was one of the most corrupt magistrates who ever cursed this country. For a gallen of whisky his deciaion could be had. He was a Governtnent spy. The Queen of England, It woman for whom he had very little re- spect, had pot given a suite of apartments in that fashion' poorhouse known as Hampton-court Palace, to Lady Mount- tomes. Lord Mountmorres was hurt in the west because he made disrespectful remarks about the F. nian, If any- one desired to epeak disrespectful about the Ferians, he should keep out of the west of Ireland. After further allu- Mona to the private life of Lord Mountmorrte, Retlpath suildenl• resumed her seat, exclaiming "That's enough." Teen toND LRAM. • Bumf, Tantart Cocoons—Than fiery Orange leader, the Rev. R. R. Kane, stigmatised the Land League as "a cowardly, wicked, and I,loodthirtv cruelde against every principle of honesty, decency, and againat even the lives of fellow creatures." Tie rev. gentle-' man .11, d upon the Government to prohibit at once the dissemination of a print called the lrish World, which " stimulates the worst and fierceet paseiens." DYNAMITE AND Greg COTTMN AS LAMDLORD MINATOPA—An orator named Nally, who addressed a land meeting at Shrule, in Mayo, openly avowed himself a rebel, and " recommended dynamite and gun cotton "as aids to the extermination of landlords. Mr. Nally's harangue was brought to on abrupt conclusion by the fall of the board on wbid, ho was standing. The omen should not be without its effect on people who advocate murder and arson.

Mr. Mrrcitat.c Hveuv has excuml himself front attend- ing a Land League meeting in Galvray in a letter in which he remarks that he was elected to give fair play to the Liberal Government, and he bolds all shams and imposters in abhorrence. The reading of Mr. Henry's otter at the meeting was received with groans, and a BAllinaske town councillor, named Matthew Harris, made a speech devoted to a denunciatien of the hon. gentleman,and was applauded thr.n.ughont. „ . . . . .

PARKehr.—On Tuesday, the freedom of the city of Limerick was presented to Mr. Parnell, who, in acknowledg- ing the gift. after referring to municipal institutions, said that during tbe last session ef Parliament the Irish parlia- mentary party had, for the first time in their parliamentary relations between England and Ireland, mccessfully resisted the attempt of British statesmen high in office to sap their independence. fearing the present short, sharp, and he hoped decisive struggle for the restoration of their legisla- tive independence, the constituencies sh..ulol support them. If the Irish members failed in their effert, thon he, for one, , would not consent to remain for an indefinite time in the English Parliament, but should esnaider it his duty to re- turn to his countrymen, and consult with them as to the further action they ought to take. It was with the people to my what other lines, what other methods, should be adopted.—At a meeting of the Kilkenny corporation, on Tuesday, emotion to confer the freedom of the city on Mr. I'arnell was propoaed, but could not be. put a qupmm not being present The meeting broke up en elisorder.w Teen Pore Ann one 181.1 LAND Qr.-110,4.—ft is stated that the Pope, having hmrel that the bishops of Galway and Waterford have spoken in favour of the land movement in Ireland, has manifested bin displeasure, and has charged Cardinal Nina, who is still discharging the functions of secretary, to obtain exact information, and if the facts he : true to renew his imperative instructious to the effect that the clergy shall in no wise meddle with mch questions save to teach peace. If this intimation does not praluce its due effect the Pope will address himself directly to the bishops in question.
